displayQuote: Success usually comes to those who are too busy to be looking for it

meta.title: Who really said "Success usually comes to those who are too busy to be looking for it"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: No — Thoreau never wrote it. The Walden Woods Project lists it as a misquotation that surfaced in the mid-20th century, decades after his death.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Success usually comes to those who are too busy to be looking for it'?
meta.ogDescription: Thoreau (d. 1862) never wrote this. Thoreau's own scholarly library lists it as a modern misquotation with no source in his works.

answer.label: Not Henry David Thoreau — a modern misquotation
answer.authorDates: Line first surfaced mid-20th century · Thoreau died 1862
answer.sourceLine: The Walden Woods Project’s official mis-quotation page lists this line and states it “started to appear in the mid-20th century in a few minor publications before proliferating on the Internet in the 21st-century.” It is found in none of Thoreau’s essays, journals, or letters, and no genuine author has been identified.

source.heading: The record
source.excerpt: Success usually comes to those who are too busy to be looking for it.
trail: Thoreau’s own scholarly library, the Walden Woods Project mis-quotation page, lists this line and dates its first appearances to the mid-20th century.
Wikiquote’s Thoreau entry does not include the line anywhere — not in its sourced, disputed, or misattributed sections.
Popular quote sites such as BrainyQuote present it as Thoreau’s with no source citation, which is how the misattribution propagates.
source.excerptNote: Widely circulated under Thoreau’s name, but absent from every one of his essays, journals, and letters.
source.rightsNote: The wording’s origin is unknown — it is not traceable to any Thoreau work or to any identified author, and the Walden Woods Project places its first appearances only in the mid-20th century. With no established source or author, no copyright status can be responsibly asserted.

author.name: Henry David Thoreau
author.heading: About Henry David Thoreau
author.bio: Henry David Thoreau was an American essayist and philosopher, author of Walden and Civil Disobedience. His genuinely quotable prose makes his name a frequent home for modern sayings he never wrote — this is one of them.

misattribution.heading: How the misattribution works
misattribution.intro: This is a textbook orphan aphorism: a punchy modern maxim with no known author, adopted by a famous 19th-century name because it sounds like something he’d say.

items.why: Quote databases (BrainyQuote, Goodreads) all attach it to Thoreau, but the Walden Woods Project lists it among his documented mis-quotations — it appears in none of his writings.
The line surfaced in “a few minor publications” in the mid-20th century, decades after Thoreau’s 1862 death, per the Walden Woods Project. No genuine author has ever been established.

misattribution.truthLine: Verdict: not Thoreau. His own scholarly library flags it as a mid-20th-century misquotation of unknown authorship.

context.heading: Why it sticks to Thoreau
lead: Thoreau is a natural lightning rod for aphorisms about work and purpose. His real writing — “the mass of men lead lives of quiet desperation,” “simplify, simplify” — is crisp, moral, and quotable, so a tidy modern maxim about success finding the busy slides comfortably under his name and rarely gets questioned.

But this particular line matches nothing in his corpus. It carries a mid-20th-century, self-improvement cadence rather than Thoreau’s 1840s–50s prose, and the earliest appearances his own scholarly library can find are minor publications well after his death.
context.pull: A modern success maxim in Thoreau’s clothing — his own library says it isn’t his.
